questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: To get far away - both geographically and culturally. I wanted to challenge myself and really broaden my horizons. I also found China particularly interesting considering the current international political landscape

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Upon arrival it was relatively easy. All university related stuff was easy enough since it was in english, but anything outside of uni was a bit more challenging due to language barriers. A lot of locals were super helpful though, so it didn't take long to figure out - you really just have to ask for help!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Some volunteers at the university helped me get my sim card upon arrival (there's a shop on campus), and all things related to university and classes were handled as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Two options for on campus housing - main building and the sub buildings. Both are good, main building is bigger, newer and more expensive. I was expecting it to be more social, but overall it was nice with your own balcony and bathroom. No sufficient kitchen options in any of the buildings though!! 

My impression is that the sub building is more social, as you share a living space with other international students, and it's also half the price (ca. 1500 dkk VS. the 3000 for a single room in main building), so that's worth considering

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
There was a kitchen, but it only had a few transportable stoves, no oven and no fridge - and also no cooking utensils, you have to buy those yourself. 

However, there's a huge cafeteria 3 mins away (still on campus) where you can get very (as in VERY) cheap and delicious meals and the variety (within chinese cuisine) is good as well. There's also a bunch of restaurants, bars and cafés nearby if you want an off-campus option.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
It's really good - close to school and you're surrounded by other international students, making it easy to meet people, so I highly recommend it. 

However, there's very limitied room, so you have to be ready the second admission for a room opens. It gets sold out within minutes, so set your alarm and be ready!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Relatively easy

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I don't remember it that well - it takes some time but is duable. Just remember to have all the documents ready in time, including a recommendation from a professor, TOEFL test etc. 

On campus registration was similar - not the most efficient and spread out on different locations and steps, but people were helpful and it was a good way to get to know campus :')

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much, you had to figure it out on your own. Fudan is terrible at answering emails, but if you show up at the international students office it usually helps a bit - and they're very friendly and helpful when you show up in person.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very succesful, I got everything I wanted

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be patient and don't be afraid to ask for help - and trust that it will all work out

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took LL.M courses, which meant that all classes were for exchange students only. It was nice, since it was catered to an exchange students needs in terms of flexibility and academic demands, but it would also have been cool to have classes with local students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Similar - seminars where the teacher presented, occasional group work and presentations.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introduction to Chinese Law
China's Practice on international law
Chinese Securities Law
Chinese Commercial Arbitration 
Chinese Legal Culture
Chinese Language

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
China's Practice on international law was very interesting for political reasons - and I actually learned a great deal. The teacher was great and the topics were very interesting - especially from a western perspective. 

Chinese Commercial Arbitration was also a highlight - it was very internationally oriented, so if you want to learn about international arbitration, it's a good option. I learned a lot and it was my most academically challenging class - in a very good way!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not many to be fair - my computer screen broke, but i was able to fix it for 900 kr. by getting a chinese speaking friend to help me. It is also worth noting that you pay your rent for the whole semester up front if you choose on housing campus, which was a bit of a surprise for me

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food can be both very cheap and expensive - the cafeteria and small whole-in-the-wall restaurants are very cheap, but you can also get expensive meals. It's easy to end up spending a lot of money because many things are cheap and you want to have a good time

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There's a lot of different clubs, however most of them are chinese speaking only. The running club was amazing!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Anything you can imagine. Martial arts, different kinds of normal art, dance, fishing, diving, soccer, sailing, music - literally everything. There's a huge fair at the beginning of the semester where you can get introduced to all the different clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The running club! I also heard great things about traditional painting and pottery.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
First of all, experience Shanghai! It's a huge city with so much to offer. Go to all the rooftops, visit the bund, the french concession, the marriage market in People's Park, Yu Garden, Jing an - i could go on forever! The food is amazing too - you have to experience hot pot at haidilao as well as xiao long bao, which originates from Shanghai. 

In terms of trips, I went to Beijing, Hangzhou Qiandao, Jiangxi/Fujian provinces round trip, Sichuan province round trip and Yunnan province round trip - and would recommend all of them. China has so much amazing nature as well as interesting cities and places to visit, and I cannot recommend enough to take advantage and explore while you're there. Shanghai is very different from the rest of China and it was incredible to experience the huge diversity in culture and landscapes throughout the country. Also, domestic flights and high speed trains are cheap and accessible so might as well!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Relatively easy, as there are many internationals on campus. However, China is very different in every single way, and it's very much a "learn as you go" experience. You get used to slurping your noodles, the loudness of everything, squat toilets everywhere, and before you know it it does not even bother you. 

I would really just recommend to go with the flow and not be too intimidated by the cultural differences and just go with the flow. It's interesting to experience, and makes for a lot of fun conversations - and soon enough, you're blending in with the locals. 

If you ever need a taste of home, Shanghai is also amazing, as it is very western compared to the rest of China. There's plenty of options for western food and vibes.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just be open. They're usually very curious and want to talk to you (and will probably approach you).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The spitting and loud phones

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food and culture of social style dining! Also, Chinese people are extremely helpful and contrary to the stereotype, not rude at all. Most of the things that gives them the perception of "rude" are cultural differences you learn to appreciate, and they're very eager to talk and help at all times.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Enjoy it so much - and again, trust that it all works out. You're in for an experience of a lifetime, so be open, curious and patient with yourself and everything around you.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring extra credit cards!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: How much confidence I gained. Moving to China on my own, making so many friends and building a wonderful life in Shanghai really boosted my confidence and has made me resilient to any challenge that may arise

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I don't remember having any great challenges - but some great advice would be to reach out to those around you and to make sure to build a good support network

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
